abstract: |
  Treemaps communicate part-of-whole relationships by mapping quantities to
  areas. Voronoi treemaps generalise the familiar rectangular layout to
  arbitrary convex boundaries and organic, polygon-shaped cells, but the
  existing R implementations delegate the layout either to a JavaScript/D3
  runtime or to compiled CGAL code, which complicates installation,
  reproducibility, and integration with the ggplot2 ecosystem. Here I present
  ggvmap, an R package that computes Voronoi map treemaps in pure R -- its
  only hard dependency is ggplot2 -- and renders them as ordinary ggplot2
  objects. ggvmap supports hierarchical (grouped) layouts, a grammar of
  pipe-able annotation layers (rings, flags, images, value labels),
  automatic small-cell label handling, and interactive hover maps. The
  tessellations it produces are exact power diagrams whose defining
  geometric properties are enforced by property-based tests. Benchmarks
  against voronoiTreemap (D3) and WeightedTreemaps (CGAL) show that ggvmap
  has the simplest installation and the shortest code for the same plot, is
  the fastest of the measurable implementations below about fifty cells,
  and trades runtime -- governed by an explicit, user-visible iteration
  budget -- at larger sizes.
keywords: [data visualization, treemap, Voronoi diagram, power diagram, R, ggplot2]
---

**Highlights**

- Voronoi map treemaps as native ggplot2 layers, in pure R with a single
  hard dependency (ggplot2).
- Hierarchical (grouped) layouts plus a grammar of pipe-able annotation
  verbs: rings (band or labelled arc), country flags, images, and value
  labels.
- Automatic small-cell handling: per-cell label autoscaling and area-based
  label suppression.
- Verified correctness: the layout is an exact power diagram, enforced by
  property-based tests on every build.

# Introduction

Part-of-whole structure is among the most common shapes of scientific data:
gene families within a genome, reads within a sequencing library, budget
positions within an economy. Treemaps display such data by making the area
of a cell proportional to its weight. The classic rectangular treemap is
easy to compute but produces high-aspect-ratio slivers and a strongly
grid-like appearance; *Voronoi treemaps* [@balzer2005] instead partition an
arbitrary convex polygon into organic cells, improving both aesthetics and
area perception, and are the layout behind many widely shared
data-journalism infographics.

Computing a Voronoi treemap requires iteratively adapting an additively
weighted Voronoi diagram -- a power diagram [@aurenhammer1987] -- until every
cell's area matches its target share [@nocaj2012]. In R, two implementations
exist: **voronoiTreemap**, which wraps the D3/JavaScript layout in an
htmlwidget [@voronoitreemap], and **WeightedTreemaps**, which computes the
layout in compiled C++ against the CGAL geometry library
[@weightedtreemaps]. Both work well, but neither produces a ggplot2 object,
and both carry installation burdens -- a browser runtime in one case, CGAL
compilation in the other -- that complicate scripted, reproducible
pipelines. There is no pure-R, ggplot2-native option. **ggvmap** fills that
gap, following the design precedent of tidyplots [@engler2025] in offering
a small, consistent, pipe-able interface on top of ggplot2 [@wickham2016].

# Results

## A grammar of Voronoi maps

@fig-design summarises the interface. A single computation function,
`voronoi_map()`, takes weights (optionally with labels and a grouping
vector) and returns the tessellation; `ggvmap()` renders it as a ggplot;
and a family of `vm_add_*()` verbs -- `vm_add_ring()`, `vm_add_labels()`,
`vm_add_flags()`, `vm_add_images()` -- add annotation layers through the
native pipe, each reading the layout from the plot object and returning a
new plot, so the layers chain without intermediate variables
(@fig-design A, C). `ggvmap()` also accepts raw weights directly,
collapsing computation and rendering into one call.

Appearance is controlled at three levels (@fig-design D): the map
(palette, fill mapping, clip shape, font family), the group (per-group
border colours for emphasis), and the cell (per-cell font faces, label
colours, and label selection). Arguments accept either a single value or a
vector named by cell or group, so emphasising one region of an otherwise
uniform map is a one-argument change. Because every result is a ggplot,
titles, themes, and extensions from the wider ggplot2 ecosystem (e.g.
markdown titles via ggtext, custom fonts via showtext) apply unchanged.

![Design of ggvmap. (A) The workflow: a weight vector (with optional
labels and a grouping variable) flows through `voronoi_map()`, which
computes the tessellation, into `ggvmap()`, which renders it; annotation
verbs are chained with R's native pipe, and the result is written to file
with `ggsave()` or made interactive with `vm_girafe()`. (B) From data to
plot: the nine lines of code shown produce the finished infographic below
them from the bundled `freshwater` dataset (columns `country`, `share`,
`region`; each country's share of global renewable freshwater resources,
2022 [@faoaquastat]). Every cell is a country with area proportional to its
share, colour and sector encode the region, values sit beneath the names
(shrunk or hidden in the smallest cells), and the outer arc ring carries
each region's total share. (C) The complete exported vocabulary, grouped by
role: one computation function; four output functions; four pipe-able
annotation verbs; accessors that return tidy data frames for custom
ggplot2 work; the colour and flag helpers; and the ten convex boundary
constructors. (D) Appearance arguments by the level they act on -- whole
map, group, or single cell. Every cell-level argument also accepts a
vector named by cell label, so emphasising one cell (bold face, different
colour, its own label) is a one-argument change with no data
manipulation.](figures/fig1_design.png){#fig-design width="100%"}

## One dataset, many maps

@fig-gallery shows the same dataset across the package's layout and
annotation space: nine convex boundary shapes, a hierarchical layout with
one sector per region and per-group border emphasis, the two ring styles
(filled band and labelled arc with group shares), continuous fill by
weight, and flag annotations. Labels in small cells are automatically
shrunk (`autoscale`) or suppressed (`min_area`), which keeps maps with
long-tailed weight distributions legible without manual tuning.

![Gallery: one dataset, fourteen maps. Rows 1--2: the ten largest
freshwater-holding countries laid out on each of the nine built-in convex
boundaries -- the identical weight vector fills any convex shape with
area-true cells, so the boundary is a free design choice. Row 3, left to
right: the full 30-row dataset in a hierarchical layout (one sector per
region) with the LATAM region singled out by a dark border
(`group_border_col = c(LATAM = "#333333")`); the filled `"band"` ring
style, where each segment spans the angular extent of its region's sector;
the thin `"arc"` ring style with each region's share appended to its label
(`values = TRUE`); continuous fill mapped to cell weight
(`fill_by = "data_weight"`), turning the map into a treemap-heatmap
hybrid; and national flags resolved automatically from the country names
(`vm_add_flags()`). Throughout, labels in small cells shrink
(`autoscale = TRUE`) or disappear below an area threshold (`min_area`),
keeping long-tailed data legible without manual
tuning.](figures/fig2_gallery.png){#fig-gallery width="100%"}

## Use cases

@fig-usecases sketches four disciplinary applications, each fully
scripted in the repository: gene families by genome share, genome-wide
association hits per chromosome, RNA-seq library composition (with the
contaminant fraction outlined for emphasis), and household expenditure
shares. The data in this figure are simulated but realistic; the scripts
are drop-in templates for real data.

![Use cases across disciplines. All data are simulated but realistic, and
each panel's complete script ships in `paper/figures/fig3_usecases.R` as a
drop-in template. (A) Genomics: twelve large gene families sized by gene
count and grouped by functional class; the arc ring reports each class's
share of the depicted families, and light-on-dark label colours keep the
dark Regulation sector readable. (B) Genetics: simulated genome-wide
association hits per human chromosome (weights roughly proportional to
chromosome length) on a rectangular boundary, with continuous fill
restating each cell's weight so hot chromosomes stand out twice -- by area
and by colour. (C) Transcriptomics: where the reads of an RNA-seq library
end up, grouped into signal, contaminant, and noise classes; the
contaminant class is outlined dark for emphasis and fractions below 2% of
the library lose their labels (`min_area`). (D) Social science: household
expenditure shares grouped by need category, the same
hierarchy-plus-arc-ring pattern as panel A applied to survey-style
data.](figures/fig3_usecases.png){#fig-usecases width="88%"}

## Benchmarks

```{r}
res <- read.csv("figures/benchmark_results.csv")
fmt_s <- function(x) ifelse(x < 1, paste0(round(x * 1000), " ms"),
                            ifelse(x < 90, paste0(round(x, 1), " s"),
                                   paste0(round(x / 60, 1), " min")))
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
gg  <- res[res$package == "ggvmap", ]
wt  <- res[res$package == "WeightedTreemaps", ]
gg10  <- gg[gg$n == 10, ];  wt10  <- wt[wt$n == 10, ]
gg50  <- gg[gg$n == 50, ];  wt50  <- wt[wt$n == 50, ]
gg100 <- gg[gg$n == 100, ]; wt100 <- wt[wt$n == 100, ]
gg500 <- gg[gg$n == 500, ]; wt500 <- wt[wt$n == 500, ]
```

@fig-benchmark compares ggvmap with voronoiTreemap and
WeightedTreemaps on four axes, each package at its default settings.
*Install complexity* (@fig-benchmark A): ggvmap needs
`r unique(gg$n_deps)` recursively resolved CRAN packages and no compiled
code, versus `r unique(wt$n_deps)` packages plus CGAL compilation for
WeightedTreemaps; voronoiTreemap resolves 44 packages and runs its layout
in a browser. *Code length* (@fig-benchmark B): the same grouped treemap
takes the fewest words, characters, and function calls in ggvmap.
*Runtime* (@fig-benchmark C) is size-dependent. On small maps ggvmap is
the faster of the two measurable implementations --
`r fmt_s(gg10$median_s)` versus `r fmt_s(wt10$median_s)` at n = 10 and
`r fmt_s(gg50$median_s)` versus `r fmt_s(wt50$median_s)` at n = 50 --
because it avoids the fixed setup cost of the compiled pipeline. Beyond
that, pure R pays its price: `r fmt_s(gg100$median_s)` versus
`r fmt_s(wt100$median_s)` at n = 100, and a
`r round(gg500$median_s / wt500$median_s)`-fold gap at n = 500
(`r fmt_s(gg500$median_s)` vs `r fmt_s(wt500$median_s)`). Treemaps
typically summarise tens of categories, where ggvmap is competitive or
faster; for maps of many hundreds of cells, WeightedTreemaps is the right
tool.

*Accuracy* (@fig-benchmark D) turns out to measure convergence, not
intrinsic layout quality. At n = 10 and n = 50 the layout converges below
the default 1% area-error threshold within 32 and 63 iterations, giving
`r pct(gg10$mean_rel_area_error)` and `r pct(gg50$mean_rel_area_error)`
mean relative cell-area error. The n = 100 and n = 500 instances exhaust
the default budget of 200 iterations before converging; the stopped
layouts show `r pct(gg100$mean_rel_area_error)` and
`r pct(gg500$mean_rel_area_error)` mean error, and the n = 100 draw --
whose lognormal weights span a 128-fold range -- is the hardest of the
four. This is an iteration-budget artefact, not a ceiling: rerunning the
same n = 100 instance with `max_iter = 500` converges after 383 iterations
to 2.3% mean error (63 s). ggvmap is deliberately transparent about this:
the returned object carries a `converged` flag and the iteration count.
WeightedTreemaps shows the same budget-dependence under its own defaults
(`r pct(min(wt$mean_rel_area_error))` to
`r pct(max(wt$mean_rel_area_error))` across sizes), and both
implementations concentrate their largest relative errors in the smallest
cells, where the target area is near zero and a large *relative* error is
visually invisible. voronoiTreemap computes its layout in the browser, so
R-side runtime and accuracy are not measurable; it appears only in panels
A--B.

![Benchmarks against the two existing R implementations, all packages at
default settings; the full protocol is in Methods and
`paper/figures/fig4_benchmark.R`. (A) Install complexity: recursively
resolved CRAN dependencies (Depends, Imports, LinkingTo; base packages
excluded). ggvmap's 17 are ggplot2 and its tree, with no compiled code;
WeightedTreemaps adds CGAL compilation; voronoiTreemap runs on the
htmlwidgets/D3 stack. (B) Code length for the same grouped treemap of
`data(freshwater)`: lines, words, characters, and function calls of the
minimal script in each package (log scale; lower is better). (C) Median
layout runtime on flat maps of lognormal(3, 1) weights, log--log axes:
ggvmap (teal) is fastest up to n = 50, then the compiled implementation
(orange) pulls ahead -- 33 s vs 5.5 s at n = 100 and 14.5 min vs 29 s at
n = 500. (D) Mean relative cell-area error, |actual - target| / target.
The ggvmap points at n = 100 and n = 500 are layouts stopped by the
default 200-iteration budget (the returned `converged` flag is `FALSE`);
the same n = 100 instance converges to 2.3% mean error given
`max_iter = 500`. Panels C--D omit voronoiTreemap, whose layout runs in
the browser and is not measurable from R.](figures/fig4_benchmark.png){#fig-benchmark width="92%"}

# Conclusion

ggvmap makes Voronoi map treemaps a first-class citizen of the ggplot2
ecosystem: a one-line install, a small pipe-able grammar, verified
geometry, and publication-style annotation layers. The pure-R
implementation trades raw speed at large cell counts for zero installation
friction and full composability -- a trade that favours the typical
treemap, which summarises tens of categories, not thousands. Its main
current limitations are the quadratic per-iteration cost of the clipping
loop, which makes maps beyond a few hundred cells slow, and the absence of
leader lines for labelling cells too small to hold text. Both are planned:
spatial indexing restricts clipping to a cell's actual neighbours and is
expected to reduce the large-map runtime by an order of magnitude without
leaving pure R, and callout labels are deferred until they can be added
without new hard dependencies.

# Methods

## Interface design

The interface follows three rules, adopting the design vocabulary of
tidyplots [@engler2025] and ggplot2 [@wickham2016]: (i) one verb per
action -- `voronoi_map()` computes, `ggvmap()` renders, `vm_add_*()`
annotate; (ii) every function both accepts and returns the natural object
of its stage (weights to layout to plot), so calls compose with the pipe;
(iii) arguments degrade gracefully from scalars to named vectors, so
emphasis is expressed by naming cells or groups rather than by
restructuring data. Annotation layers re-attach the layout object to the
returned plot, which is what makes the chain stateless for the user.

## Algorithm

The layout follows @nocaj2012. Each cell is a site with a position and an
additive power weight; the plane is partitioned by the power diagram
[@aurenhammer1987], computed here in pure R by sequential half-plane
clipping of the convex boundary. Each iteration moves every site to its
cell's centroid (position adaptation) and multiplicatively adjusts its
power weight by the ratio of target to actual area (weight adaptation),
until the maximum relative area error falls below a convergence threshold.
Intuitively, the algorithm is a room full of balloons: each balloon drifts
toward the centre of its territory and inflates or deflates until it holds
exactly its share of the room. Hierarchical maps solve the group-level
map first, then run the same algorithm inside each group polygon -- a valid
nested power diagram. Weights are initialised proportional to target areas
and sites by farthest-point sampling, which removes degenerate starts.
Iteration stops when the maximum relative area error falls below
`convergence_ratio` (default 1%) or after `max_iter` iterations (default
200); the returned object records both the iteration count and a
`converged` flag, so an unconverged layout is never silent -- rerunning
with a larger `max_iter` or a different `seed` resolves it.

## Correctness

The test suite enforces the defining properties of the output rather than
snapshots: every point of a fine grid lies in the cell of its
minimum-power-distance site; cell areas sum to the clip area to machine
precision with no gaps or overlaps; every cell is convex; and each
hierarchical subcell lies inside its group polygon
(`tests/testthat/test-correctness.R`). These property-based tests run on
every build.

## Dependencies

ggvmap Imports only ggplot2 (plus the base packages grDevices, stats,
utils). Optional features degrade gracefully behind `requireNamespace()`
guards: ggimage (flags, images), ggiraph (interactivity), geomtextpath
(curved ring labels), magick and png (image caching).

## Benchmarking

Benchmarks (@fig-benchmark) were run with bench [@bench]: flat maps
of n = 10, 50, 100, 500 lognormal(3, 1) weights, median of 10 iterations
(3 at n = 500), on a single laptop core, each package at its default
settings (for ggvmap: `convergence_ratio = 0.01`, `max_iter = 200`,
`min_weight_ratio = 0.01`). Layouts that reach `max_iter` unconverged are
reported as measured; the text notes where a larger budget converges
them. Dependency counts are recursive Depends, Imports and
LinkingTo on CRAN, excluding base packages. Code-length metrics count
lines, words, characters, and function calls of the minimal code producing
the same grouped treemap in each package. Layout accuracy is the mean over
cells of |actual - target| / target area, taken from each package's
reported per-cell areas. The full script is
`paper/figures/fig4_benchmark.R`; results are archived in
`paper/figures/benchmark_results.csv`.

## Data availability

ggvmap is available at https://github.com/loukesio/ggvmap under the MIT
licence. The `freshwater` dataset ships with the package (FAO Aquastat via
World Bank, 2022 [@faoaquastat]). All figures in this paper are generated
by the scripts in `paper/figures/` and rendered by `paper/render.R`.
